title: Numbers, promotion, overflow and exactness
outcome: Choose and validate numeric representations while distinguishing exact arithmetic, overflow and floating-point approximation.
key_terms: Fixed-width integer arithmetic wraps around silently when an exact result exceeds the type's range, giving a wrong value without an error.
Functions such as `Base.Checked.checked_add` that throw an `OverflowError` instead of wrapping when the exact result does not fit.
The 64-bit binary floating-point type whose values such as `0.1` are rounded approximations, so comparisons need a stated tolerance.
An exact fraction type built with `//`, such as `1//3`, that stores an integer numerator and denominator.
The rule that converts mixed numeric arguments to a common type before arithmetic, so an `Int` plus a `Float64` gives a `Float64`.
approach: Pick the numeric type from the question being asked. Integer division and remainder use `div` and `rem`; exact ratios use `Rational`; values past `typemax(Int)` need `BigInt` before the operation; and floating-point checks use tolerances tied to units. Every conversion that cannot hold its value should fail loudly rather than wrap.

exercises.title: Retain a remainder
exercises.task: Compute quotient and remainder for 7 divided by 2.
exercises.expected: The integer quotient is 3 and remainder 1.
exercises.answer: Integer division answers another question from floating-point division.
exercises.why: Seven equals 2 times 3 plus 1, so `div(7, 2)` returns 3 and `rem(7, 2)` returns 1, both as integers.
exercises.wrong: Writing `7 / 2` and truncating the float answers a different question; it returns 3.5 and loses the remainder unless it is recomputed separately.
exercises.verify: Assert `div(7, 2) == 3` and `rem(7, 2) == 1`; the reference already checks `rem(7, 2) == 1`.

exercises.title: Reject a narrowing conversion
exercises.answer: A constructor conversion that cannot represent the value must not be confused with wrapping arithmetic.
exercises.why: `Int8` covers -128 through 127, so the constructor `Int8(128)` has no exact result and throws `InexactError`.
exercises.wrong: Expecting -128 confuses conversion with wrapping arithmetic; `typemax(Int8) + Int8(1)` wraps, but a checked constructor refuses an unrepresentable value.
exercises.verify: Use `@test_throws InexactError Int8(128)` as the reference does, then confirm `Int8(127)` succeeds.

exercises.title: Keep an exact ratio
exercises.answer: This preserves the intended ratio instead of first rounding decimal-looking binary floats.
exercises.why: `1//10 + 2//10` is computed as integer numerators over a common denominator, giving `3//10` with no rounding at any step.
exercises.wrong: Using `0.1 + 0.2` and comparing with `0.3` fails, because both decimals are rounded binary floats and the sum is `0.30000000000000004`.
exercises.verify: Check `1//10 + 2//10 == 3//10` and, for contrast, `0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3`, which is false.

exercises.title: Choose a precision
exercises.expected: Their types are Float32 and Float64.
exercises.hint: Literal syntax is part of the contract.
exercises.answer: More precision changes representation cost and error; it does not validate the model.
exercises.why: The suffix `f0` makes `1.0f0` a `Float32`; plain `1.0` is `Float64`, with roughly 7 versus 16 significant decimal digits.
exercises.wrong: Treating the two literals as the same value with different spelling ignores precision; `eps(1.0f0)` is about 1.2e-7 while `eps(1.0)` is about 2.2e-16.
exercises.verify: Print `typeof(1.0f0)` and `typeof(1.0)`; the reference asserts `typeof(1.0f0) == Float32`.

exercises.title: Check a large integer
exercises.expected: The mathematical integer is retained beyond the machine Int range.
exercises.answer: Converting a wrapped machine result afterward cannot reconstruct the lost value.
exercises.why: `BigInt(2)^100` promotes before multiplying, so the exact 31-digit value survives; machine `2^100` wraps modulo 2 to the 64 and yields 0.
exercises.wrong: Computing `2^100` first and calling `BigInt` on the result gives `BigInt(0)`, since the overflow happened before the conversion.
exercises.verify: Assert `BigInt(2)^100 > typemax(Int)` as the reference does, and print `2^100` beside it to see the wrapped 0.

exercises.title: Explain a tolerance
exercises.task: Justify an absolute tolerance for a measured quantity.
exercises.expected: The bound uses that quantity units and required accuracy.
exercises.hint: Do not substitute a larger bound for a diagnosis.
exercises.answer: Representation, conditioning and algorithmic error inform a tolerance; passing an arbitrary bound proves little.
exercises.why: A measured length in meters with a stated 1 millimeter requirement justifies an absolute tolerance of 0.001, tied to units rather than to float precision alone.
exercises.wrong: Raising `atol` until a failing comparison passes hides whether the error came from representation, conditioning or a wrong formula.
exercises.verify: Write the tolerance next to its unit and source, then confirm `isapprox(x, y; atol = 0.001)` fails for a deliberately perturbed value.
